\chapter{Which One in the Line}
\label{ch:gu-ordinals}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say first to fifth in Gujarati, agree any of them with a masculine, feminine or neuter thing, and say which one of the five the language builds rather than hands down.}

Complete GU-R38-first-to-fifth and run pahelun to paanchmun, then say which one of the five you could have worked out.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[pā̃chmũ]{\gu{પાંચમું} (pā̃chmũ) — fifth, and the ending you can see}

\label{lesson:GU-C38-panchmu}



\begin{quote}
A second kind of number word starts here, so the recalls come first.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{how many} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{who} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{because} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{મહિનો}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{પાંચ}, with something behind it}
\textbf{\gu{કેટલા}} counts things, and \textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}} answer it. A number can also answer \emph{which one in the line}, and \textbf{\gu{કેટલા}} does not reach that. \textbf{\gu{પાંચ} \gu{ચા}} is five teas; picking the last cup out of a row is a different job.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} — \emph{pā̃chmũ} — \textbf{fifth}
\end{quote}

Look at it before anything is said about it. \textbf{\gu{પાંચ}} is still there, whole, and \textbf{-\gu{મું}} sits behind it.

That \textbf{-\gu{ું}} is the neuter you met on \textbf{\gu{મારું}}, so this word agrees like any other:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{gender} & \textbf{fifth} \\
\midrule
masculine & \textbf{\gu{પાંચમો}} — \emph{pā̃chmo} \\
feminine & \textbf{\gu{પાંચમી}} — \emph{pā̃chmī} \\
neuter & \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} — \emph{pā̃chmũ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\gu{મહિનો}} is masculine, so the fifth month is \textbf{\gu{પાંચમો} \gu{મહિનો}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: an ending that keeps working}]
\textbf{-\gu{મું}} is not a one-off. Wiktionary's entry for the suffix builds the ordinal of every Gujarati number with it except five: \textbf{\gu{એક}}, \textbf{\gu{બે}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, \textbf{\gu{ચાર}}, and the word for six, which the next chapter reaches.

That list lands well for you. Your count stops at \textbf{\gu{પાંચ}}, so of the five ordinals you can reach at all, \textbf{four stand on the exception list and one does not}. This chapter is that exception list, plus the single word showing what the exceptions are exceptions to.

Which is \textbf{\gu{કેમકે}} the chapter starts at the far end rather than at \emph{first}: a broken shape stays unreadable until the shape has been seen.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pā̃ch chā}, then \emph{pā̃chmũ}
  \item \emph{pā̃chmo}, \emph{pā̃chmī}, \emph{pā̃chmũ}
  \item \emph{pā̃chmo mahino}, and write \textbf{\gu{મહિનો}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which question does \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} answer, and which one does \textbf{\gu{કેટલા}} answer? (\emph{Which one in the line}; \emph{how many}.) How many of the five stand on the exception list? (\textbf{Four.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AA\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%82\%E0\%AA\%9A\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{પાંચમું}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: -\gu{મું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[trījũ]{\gu{ત્રીજું} (trījũ) — third, and the first word that will not take -\gu{મું}}

\label{lesson:GU-C38-triju}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls before the second ordinal arrives.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fifth}, and the two pieces in it — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{where} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{why}, then answer \emph{because} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{અત્યારે}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{ત્રીજું}}
The suffix entry named \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}} among the numbers \textbf{-\gu{મું}} does not build on. So the ordinal of three is not \textbf{\gu{ત્રણમું}}, and the book owes you the word it is.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} — \emph{trījũ} — \textbf{third}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, then \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}}. The opening \textbf{\gu{ત્ર}} carries over untouched — including the \textbf{r} that chapter twelve made a fuss about, the one Gujarati put back where Hindi has none. Only the tail differs.

Endings as before: \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજો}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજી}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} down from Old Gujarati \emph{trījaũ}, and that from Sanskrit \emph{tṛtīya}. Notice what is missing from that line: no suffix, no addition, no \textbf{-\gu{મું}} in it anywhere.

\textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} was described as something Gujarati \emph{makes}. \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} is described as something Gujarati \emph{received}. Two ordinals in, and the dictionary is already sorting them into two piles.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{traṇ}, then \emph{trījũ}
  \item \emph{pā̃chmũ}, then \emph{trījũ} — built, then received
  \item \emph{trījo}, \emph{trījī}, \emph{trījũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What can you still see of \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}} inside \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}}? (\textbf{The opening \gu{ત્ર}, r and all.}) Which of your two ordinals was assembled from parts? (\textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A4\%E0\%AB\%8D\%E0\%AA\%B0\%E0\%AB\%80\%E0\%AA\%9C\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{ત્રીજું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bījũ]{\gu{બીજું} (bījũ) — second, other, and a shape with two members}

\label{lesson:GU-C38-biju}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the second half of a pair.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{third} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{ક્યાં}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{કેમકે}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the eight time words — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{બીજું}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{બીજું}} — \emph{bījũ} — \textbf{second}, and also \textbf{other}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\gu{બે}}, then \textbf{\gu{બીજું}}. Almost nothing survives the crossing. One consonant does: the \textbf{b} that opens both.

Chapter twelve spent a lesson on that \textbf{b}. Gujarati took the feminine-and-neuter \emph{dvé} side of the Sanskrit paradigm, and \emph{dv} went to \emph{bb} and then to \emph{b}, which is why \textbf{\gu{બે}} does not begin like Hindi \emph{do}. The ordinal begins the way the cardinal does.

Endings as before: \textbf{\gu{બીજો}}, \textbf{\gu{બીજી}}, \textbf{\gu{બીજું}}. The everyday sense of \textbf{other} sits in the same word — the \emph{other} cup, the \emph{other} road — exactly as \emph{second} and \emph{other} share one word in English.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: two words, one shape}]
Set the two received ordinals side by side and the tails match:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ordinal} & \textbf{Sanskrit source Wiktionary gives} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\gu{બીજું}} — \emph{bījũ} & \emph{dvitīya} \\
\textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} — \emph{trījũ} & \emph{tṛtīya} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two Sanskrit words that ended alike, in \emph{-tīya}, came down as two Gujarati words that end alike, in \textbf{-\gu{ીજું}}. The exceptions to \textbf{-\gu{મું}} are not a heap of unrelated oddments; at least two of them are one another's company.

They are not equally readable, though. \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} still shows its number and \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} does not, and that is the order this chapter walks: the number fades word by word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{be}, then \emph{bījũ}
  \item \emph{bījũ}, \emph{trījũ} — the pair, back to back
  \item \emph{bījo}, \emph{bījī}, \emph{bījũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is left of \textbf{\gu{બે}} inside \textbf{\gu{બીજું}}? (\textbf{The b, and nothing else.}) How many shapes are on the table now? (\textbf{Two: -\gu{મું} and -\gu{ીજું}.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AC\%E0\%AB\%80\%E0\%AA\%9C\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{બીજું}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A4\%E0\%AB\%8D\%E0\%AA\%B0\%E0\%AB\%80\%E0\%AA\%9C\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{ત્રીજું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chothũ]{\gu{ચોથું} (chothũ) — fourth, and a shape that stands alone}

\label{lesson:GU-C38-chothu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the fourth.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{second}, and the ending it shares — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{when} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{for, in order to} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{ચોથું}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} — \emph{chothũ} — \textbf{fourth}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\gu{ચાર}}, then \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}}. The \textbf{\gu{ચ}} stays; the \textbf{\gu{ા}} does not. Half a consonant of the number is left, which puts this word between the two you already hold — more than \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} keeps, less than \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} keeps.

Endings as before: \textbf{\gu{ચોથો}}, \textbf{\gu{ચોથી}}, \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: three shapes, one of them alone}]
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} down from Old Gujarati \emph{caüthaũ}, from Prakrit \emph{caüttha}, from Sanskrit \emph{caturthá}. That Sanskrit word ends in \emph{-tha}, and \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} still ends in \textbf{\gu{થ}}. So the tally, four ordinals in:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{words} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-\gu{મું}}, on the whole number & \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} \\
\textbf{-\gu{ીજું}} & \textbf{\gu{બીજું}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} \\
\textbf{-\gu{થું}} & \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three shapes, and the third has a single member. \textbf{\gu{માટે}} this book does not call it a pattern: one word is not a pattern, and saying otherwise would cost you more than it saved.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chār}, then \emph{chothũ}
  \item \emph{bījũ}, \emph{trījũ}, \emph{chothũ} — three words, three tails
  \item \emph{chotho}, \emph{chothī}, \emph{chothũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What survives of \textbf{\gu{ચાર}} inside \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}}? (\textbf{The \gu{ચ}.}) How many words share its tail so far? (\textbf{None.}) Which ordinal was built rather than received? (\textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9A\%E0\%AB\%8B\%E0\%AA\%A5\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{ચોથું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pahelũ]{\gu{પહેલું} (pahelũ) — first, arriving last, and why}

\label{lesson:GU-C38-pahelu}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the word this chapter has been walking towards.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fourth} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{how many} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{therefore} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{પહેલું}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} — \emph{pahelũ} — \textbf{first}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\gu{એક}}, then \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}}. Not one sound crosses over. \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} kept \textbf{\gu{ત્ર}}, \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} kept \textbf{\gu{ચ}}, \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} kept a \textbf{b} — and this word keeps nothing at all.

Endings as before: \textbf{\gu{પહેલો}}, \textbf{\gu{પહેલી}}, \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}}. It carries an everyday second use too: \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} can mean \textbf{before}, in the sense of \emph{earlier}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here is the thing worth waiting four lessons for.

Sanskrit built \emph{first} and \emph{fifth} with the \textbf{same ending}: its words were \emph{prathamá} and \emph{pañcama}, both in \emph{-ma}. Wiktionary traces Gujarati's \textbf{-\gu{મું}} to \emph{-maka}, an extension of that same \emph{-ma}, and cites \emph{pañcamaka} as the form it comes from.

So \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} and \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} set out from one place. Then the roads part:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{stage} & \textbf{\emph{first}} \\
\midrule
Sanskrit & \emph{prathamá} \\
Ashokan Prakrit & \emph{prathilla} — the \emph{m} is now \emph{ll} \\
Sauraseni Prakrit & \emph{pahila} \\
\textbf{Gujarati} & \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The \textbf{\gu{લ}} you can see and say stands where the \textbf{m} used to be. \textbf{\gu{તેથી}} the one ordinal with no number left in it is also the one that began with the very ending you learned first, and lost it on the way.

Chapter twelve showed a sound lost and then put back. This is the opposite case: lost, left lost, and lived off ever since.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ek}, then \emph{pahelũ} — and notice nothing carries over
  \item \emph{prathamá}, \emph{prathilla}, \emph{pahila}, \emph{pahelũ}
  \item \emph{pahelo}, \emph{pahelī}, \emph{pahelũ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How much of \textbf{\gu{એક}} is in \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}}? (\textbf{None.}) What became of the Sanskrit ending in it? (\textbf{Prakrit made it an l.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AA\%E0\%AA\%B9\%E0\%AB\%87\%E0\%AA\%B2\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{પહેલું}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: -\gu{મું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{First to fifth, in order at last}

\label{lesson:GU-R38-first-to-fifth}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{first} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fifth}, and its two pieces — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{if} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here. This lesson is the first time the five stand in numerical order, and that has been deliberate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pahelũ bījũ trījũ chothũ pā̃chmũ} — the run, without stopping
  \item the four that had to be memorised, and the one that did not
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter, in one number}]
Of the five ordinals in this chapter, \textbf{one} was built and \textbf{four} were received. That is the worst ratio Gujarati will ever hand you, and it is worth saying out loud, along with why: your count reaches \textbf{\gu{પાંચ}}, and Wiktionary's own suffix entry sets aside \textbf{\gu{એક}}, \textbf{\gu{બે}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, \textbf{\gu{ચાર}} and six as the numbers \textbf{-\gu{મું}} does not build on. Four of the five words you can reach are on that list. The ratio is not a fact about Gujarati ordinals; it is a fact about where the count currently stops.

The received four do not scatter. Two of them, \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} and \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}}, share one shape; \textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} has its own; \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} ends in the \textbf{\gu{લ}} that Prakrit put where Sanskrit had an \textbf{m}.

\textbf{\gu{જો}} this book takes the count past five, the balance turns over at once — because from there on, the ordinal is the number with \textbf{-\gu{મું}} behind it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the five was assembled? (\textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}.}) Why were the other four not? (\textbf{They stand on the suffix entry's exception list.}) Which of them kept the least of its number? (\textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} — \textbf{nothing at all}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
